answer:
What I ran: a random circuit on 8 connected Garnet qubits (QB3, QB4, QB5, QB6, QB8, QB9, QB10, QB11). It has 10 layers. Each layer applies a random single-qubit rotation on every qubit, then 3 CZ gates on neighbouring qubits, so 30 CZ gates in total. I submitted it once with 1000 shots to garnet:mock (job 01a16062-7376-73b4-ab39-d861fd6fad0d). I computed the ideal output probabilities for the same circuit on my laptop with an exact state-vector simulation, then scored the samples with linear XEB.

Numbers: xeb_ideal is 1.229. This is the score a perfect quantum computer would get, and it is close to the textbook value of about 1 for random circuits. xeb_measured is -0.446. A score of 0 is what pure random guessing gives.

What the score means: linear XEB is 2^n times the average ideal probability of the bitstrings you actually measured, minus 1. A random circuit makes some bitstrings much more likely than others. A perfect device lands on the likely ones more often, so it scores near 1. A fully noisy device samples uniformly and scores 0. A score between 0 and 1 means the device is partly working, and real chips are scored this way.

Why my measured score is negative: garnet:mock is a free test device and does not simulate the circuit. It returned 8 canned bitstrings (all-zeros, all-ones, and a few mixed patterns) in roughly equal numbers. Those patterns have no link to my circuit's output, and they happen to land on bitstrings the circuit made unlikely. The -0.446 therefore shows the mock output is unrelated to the circuit. It is not a measure of Garnet's quality. A real Garnet run would be needed to get a genuine XEB, and I did not spend credits on one because you asked for the mock.

Why 8 qubits is easy for a laptop and 50 or more is not: the exact output of 8 qubits is a list of 2^8 = 256 probabilities. Computing it took well under a second. Each added qubit doubles the list. At 50 qubits it is 2^50, about 10^15 numbers, which needs roughly 16 petabytes of memory at 16 bytes per number, and that is more than almost any computer has. Clever tricks (tensor networks, sampling shortcuts) help, but their cost still grows very fast as depth and width grow. XEB itself needs the ideal probabilities, so checking a 50+ qubit device by this method is itself the hard part. That is the basis of the claim that quantum hardware beats supercomputers at this sampling task, because the quantum chip draws the samples directly while the classical computer must grind through the exponentially large calculation.
